newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian retail reversal fuels rate cut talk.
newsitem.headline: Australian retail reversal fuels rate cut talk.

text.p: Australia's retail sector may have celebrated a false dawn earlier this year, judging by data released on Friday which cast doubt on the sustainability of the strength of a rebound seen in first quarter consumption.

Retail trade fell by 1.7 percent in April, well below the median forecast of a 0.5 percent rise and over three times worse than the most pessimistic forecast of a 0.5 percent fall in a Reuters survey of 29 economists before the data release. @ The fall was seen justifying the Reserve Bank of Australia's (RBA) decision to cut rates last week, and set the market talking on the likelihood of another cut in official rates.
"It certainly indicates weakness in the economy," Colonial State Bank group economist Hans Kunnen said, adding, "it certainly throws open the prospect of further rate cuts."
April's fall followed a 0.3 percent fall in March, making it the first time retail trade has fallen in consecutive months since July and August of 1993.

Adding to the concerns about consumption was a 6.0 percent fall in April new motor vehicle registrations, although this was mitigated by the fact that registrations had risen by almost 10 percent in the forst three months of 1997.
The fall was seen justifying the Reserve Bank of Australia's (RBA) decision to cut rates last week, and set the market talking on the likelihood of another cut in official rates.
"It certainly indicates weakness in the economy," Colonial State Bank group economist Hans Kunnen. "It certainly throws open the prospect of further rate cuts," he added.
Westpac chief economist Nigel Stapledon said the figures were disappointing, and that he had expected both retail trade and car registrations to have held up better.
"It's continuing a pretty patchy picture for the economy and very much justifies the decision by the Reserve Bank to move last week cutting rates," Stapledon said.
The RBA caught the markets off-guard last week when it cut the official cash rate by 0.5 percentage points to 5.5 percent.
At the time the move was considered a surprise because of the RBA's stated optimistic outlook and the strength seen in partial indicators such as consumption.
"It's got to now cast some doubts on the sustainability on the bounce in Q1 of private consumption," HSBC Markets economist Anthony Thompson said of the April retail data.

As the strength in consumption, with its flow-through effects to jobs and production, was seen as one of the reasons to be optimistic on the economy's propects, signs of renewed weakness raised the prospects of further rate cuts.

"It will definitely add to speculation of another cut, because it's a case of if the consumer doesn't come in, employment will never kick in," Citibank Australia senior economist Annette Beacher said.

That talk weighed heavily on the Australian dollar. After rising through the morning to a week high US$0.7682 after rumours of a rate cut this morning proved false, the dollar fell to a low of US$0.7617 soon after the retail data were released.
Debt markets reacted more favourably, with the yield on 10-year bonds rallying over 10 points to under 7.50 percent.

Bill futures also rallied, with the September contract moving from an implied yield of 5.37 percent from being near the 5.5 percent official cash rate before the data, as the market began to factor in the chance of another cut.
